initial_presentation: A 32-year-old woman with no prior medical conditions presented with primary amenorrhea and has been experiencing chronic and cyclic pelvic pain since the age of 12. The patient reported not having any gynecological history or sexual activity and had never sought medical attention before due to financial constraints and limited accessibility to healthcare. During the clinical examination, the patient had a normal physical appearance and well-developed secondary sexual characteristics. Additionally, a hard and painful pelvic mass was detected. Examination of the vulvo-perineal area revealed normal external genitalia, including well-defined labia majora, labia minora, and clitoris, but there was an absence of a vaginal opening.

A 21-month-old male child, born to a nonconsanguineous couple, exhibited developmental delay and occasional limb stiffness. He was delivered at full term with a birth weight of 3.2 kg without complications. The child had not achieved neck holding, intermittently opened his palms but had not developed a palmar grasp. He displayed stranger anxiety and responded to his name. He cooed but did not produce syllables. Hearing and vision were normal. There was no history of encephalopathy, seizures, diurnal variation of symptoms, or autonomic instability. No family history of similar issues was reported. On examination, his weight was 11.2 kg (-0.12SD), length was 92 cm (+2.76SD), and head circumference was 44.3 cm (-2.54SD). Physical features included bifrontal narrowing, abnormally shaped ear pinna, depression over the helix, high arched palate, non-paralytic convergent squint in the left eye, and pes planus. He exhibited spasticity and dystonia in all limbs. Muscle power was 3/5 (MRC grade) across all muscle groups, and deep tendon reflexes were brisk.

A 4-month-old male patient was transferred to our institute due to weakness and reduced movement in the left lower extremity. He was born following an uneventful pregnancy and delivery and was in good health until one month prior to the visit when his parents observed the weakness. He had received OPV with DTaP at a local health center one month before these symptoms appeared. Initially, his parents delayed seeking appropriate medical help and took him to an orthopedics clinic where he was evaluated and treated. His family history and past medical history, including the perinatal period, were unremarkable. At the time of the report (2 years old), his body weight was 8.1 kg, length 66 cm, and head circumference 41.2 cm, with growth index measurements in the 50-90th percentile. Vital signs were unremarkable. Physical examination showed an alert mental status, and cranial nerve function tests were normal. Neurologic examination revealed significantly decreased spontaneous movement and flaccid paralysis in the left lower extremity (GI/V) with knee jerk (+/-), biceps tendon reflex (+/+), and ankle clonus (-/-). The response to painful stimuli in the left lower extremity was markedly reduced, but normal in other parts of his body. There was no history of intramuscular injection or trauma in the left buttock area.

A 32-year-old male presented to Seoul National University Dental Hospital for evaluation and management of bilateral nodular lesions on the neck, which had been present for several months. Previously, he had visited a local plastic surgery clinic due to a large lesion and pain in the right cervical area. Records from the clinic indicated that he had undergone a drainage procedure but declined surgical removal of the lesions. The patient reported that the pain and swelling decreased following the aspiration. His medical history includes cardiac septal defect repair at 10 months of age, and he reported no family history of similar skin lesions.

A 36-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with a primary complaint of toothache in the lower right posterior quadrant persisting for the past 6 months. The patient also reported having had a mobile tooth extracted in that area. An orthopantomogram was performed, which showed a radiolucent area extending from the right second premolar (45) to the socket of the previously extracted second molar (47).

A 47-year-old male presented with swelling in the left eye for 2 months, which has been gradually increasing and is associated with pain and redness. There is a swelling near the limbus on the temporal side for the past 1.5 months, also gradually increasing in size, with redness and intermittent mild pain. The patient reported no history of trauma or systemic illness such as fever, joint pains, or recent weight loss. He has been using topical antibiotics and lubricating eye drops for 2 months.

A 12-year-old boy presented with back pain persisting for 2 years. His medical history includes bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and multiple joint contractures in both wrists and fingers, particularly in the proximal interphalangeal joint of the left fifth finger. He has two male cousins with similar physical features. His parents and sister do not exhibit any noticeable anomalies. Physical examination showed facial characteristics such as micrognathia, frontal bossing, a prominent supraorbital ridge, and hypertelorism. Additional findings included hypodontia, underdevelopment of the left fifth digital phalanx and great toes, and thoracic scoliosis. The intrinsic muscles of both hands were graded 2/5 on the manual muscle test, with no sensory impairment. Knee and ankle reflexes were hyperactive, and ankle clonus was present. His height was 154 cm (63.9 percentile).

A newborn male, delivered vaginally at full term (40 weeks gestation) with a birth weight of 3115 grams, presented with a mass composed of several nodules located on the maxillary gingiva. The mass, which was approximately 2 cm at its largest dimension, was surgically removed. Upon examination, the cross-section of the mass appeared whitish-yellow and had a notably smooth surface.
A 42-year-old male reported a 6-year history of mild evening fatigue in all four limbs, followed by a gradual onset of gait imbalance and recurrent double vision.

A 25-year-old male presented with a 2-year history of red and peeling inflammation of the lips with pustules. The lesions did not improve with multiple treatment cycles using corticosteroids and emollients. Clinical examination revealed that the upper lip was red, cracked, and covered with thick white-yellowish scales along with small, non-merging pustules. The rest of the skin examination was normal, and there were no lesions on the oral mucosa, tongue, or nails. The patient was otherwise in good health. He reported no personal or family history of psoriasis or other skin conditions and no history of smoking. He denied any history of lip licking or contact with lipstick, topical antibiotics and steroids, or other cosmetics.
